B-9, as amended, including Part 17.1 Beneficial Ownership Transparency provisions; Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) for passive income and royalty characterization

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary Public in the residential jurisdiction of the ultimate beneficial owner, authenticated by the competent authority for apostilles

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary Public or Certified Legal Professional in the country of origin

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all directors, shareholders, UBOs, and authorized signatories against FINTRAC, Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, U.S. OFAC SDN, UK HMT, UN Security Council Consolidated Lists, and all Canadian sanctions regulations issued under the Special Economic Measures Act and Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act. Enhanced due diligence required for all politically exposed persons, irrespective of country of residence, before any engagement or filing.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry — Online Corporate Registration and NUANS Name Search
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: An Alberta ULC name must be in English or French and must contain the legal element 'Unlimited Liability Corporation' or the abbreviation 'ULC' as the corporate designation. Names may include numerals, letters, accents, punctuation, and distinctiveness elements, but must be clearly distinguishable from existing names in the NUANS database. Transliteration is accepted for names derived from non-Latin scripts provided a NUANS-compliant English or French rendering is submitted.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If a proposed name is rejected, the applicant or its authorized agent must submit a written reconsideration request to the Alberta Corporate Registry Name Review Committee within 30 days of rejection, attaching the original NUANS report and legal argument. If reconsideration fails, an appeal may be filed in the Alberta Court of King's Bench under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta), with a Notice of Appeal accompanied by supporting affidavits and legal submissions, and the court may issue a binding order directing the registry to accept the name.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office is permissible as the address of the registered office provided it is a physical street address in Alberta, is accessible to the public for service of process, and is not a post-office box. However, the use of a purely virtual office will not satisfy Canada Revenue Agency or FINTRAC's commercial substance requirements for an intellectual-property holding company engaged in royalty sub-licensing; minimum operational presence and discretionary documentation to evidence principal-and-agent substance must be maintained.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low for routine corporate registry matters, but FINTRAC and CRA may conduct unannounced on-site compliance inspections for medium-risk enhanced AML/CFT files; the quantified annual likelihood for this particular industry is estimated at 5% based on active ULC holding company audits and enhanced AML screening triggers.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c. B-9, ss. 12, 15, 101 and 124; Business Corporations Act regulations, Alta Reg. 186/2000; Income Tax Act (Canada), RSC 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 89(1) and 123 for ULC tax classification and unlimited liability treatment
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Corporate Registry, Service Alberta, Government of Alberta
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation (Form 3) filed with the Director of Corporate Registry, with Certificate of Incorporation issued upon approval
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital for an Alberta ULC and no escrow account requirement. Shares may be issued for nominal consideration provided the consideration is fixed by the first directors and is fully paid before issuance.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED, that the Corporation accept the subscriptions of the incorporators for the classes of shares authorized in the Articles of Incorporation, and allot and issue such shares upon payment in full of the consideration fixed by the board. RESOLVED, that the registered office of the Corporation be established at [Registered Office Address], Alberta, and that the secretary be and is hereby authorized to file all required notices of registered office and any changes with the Corporate Registry. RESOLVED, that [Name] be appointed President and Chief Executive Officer, [Name] be appointed Secretary, and [Name] be appointed Treasurer, each to serve until successors are elected. RESOLVED, that the execution and delivery of all documents necessary to give effect to these resolutions be hereby authorized, ratified and confirmed.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporate Registry, Service Alberta; NUANS search through an authorized service provider or the Alberta Corporate Registry online portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a NUANS name search to confirm that the proposed ULC name is distinguishable from existing corporate names and registered trademarks. File a name reservation request with the Corporate Registry and pay the applicable reservation fee. The reservation is valid for 90 days during which the Articles of Incorporation must be filed.
required_dossiers: NUANS name search report dated within the preceding 90 days
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the proposed name is rejected or confused with an existing name, select the second or third candidate from the NUANS report and submit a new name reservation request. The rejected search fee is not refundable, but the reservation fee may be reapplied to a new filing in limited circumstances.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation and approval of Articles of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: First director and authorized legal counsel; filing submitted to Corporate Registry, Service Alberta
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare the Articles of Incorporation in prescribed Form 3, selecting the unlimited liability corporation structure, authorized share classes, director names, and initial registered office address. Obtain each first director's consent to act. The articles must be executed by the incorporator and, for an Alberta ULC, must comply with the unlimited liability disclosure requirements.
required_dossiers: Completed and executed Form 3 Articles of Incorporation
Consent to act as first director for each named director
Registered office address and municipal confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Corporate Registry queries the articles for omitted or inconsistent particulars, amend the articles and resubmit. Deficiencies concerning director consents or share structure may be cured by filing a correction dated before the original submission, where permitted by registry practice.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Filing of Articles of Incorporation with Corporate Registry
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporate Registry, Service Alberta; online filing through authorized registry agent or corporate service provider
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit the executed Articles of Incorporation and prescribed registration fee to the Corporate Registry. The registry reviews the filing for statutory completeness, issues a Certificate of Incorporation, and assigns a Alberta corporate number. The existence of the ULC commences on the date shown in the certificate.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Corporate Registry issues a notice of deficiency, cure the stated defect by filing an amendment or correcting the articles within the registry's prescribed response period. If the application is rejected, resubmit the entire package with the registry's written directions; no substantive fee refund is available.

step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Download or obtain the Certificate of Incorporation from the Corporate Registry. Verify the exact corporate name, registered office address, and date of incorporation. The certificate is conclusive evidence of the ULC's existence and is the foundational document for all downstream governance and registrations.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the certificate contains an error, submit a written request for correction to the Director of Corporate Registry with supporting evidence. Clerical errors are normally corrected without requiring a new incorporation.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First board meeting and corporate governance formalities
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of directors of the Alberta ULC; internal corporate records maintained at the registered office
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the first board meeting to adopt by-laws, confirm the share subscription and issuance, appoint officers, establish the fiscal year end, choose the auditor or waive audit where permitted, authorize bank accounts, and ratify the incorporation expenses. Prepare signed minutes and maintain a statutory minute book.
required_dossiers: Minutes of the first board meeting
Share subscription forms and share certificates
Registered office consent and officer acceptance forms
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If directors or shareholders object to any first-board action after the meeting, reconvene the board and vote on a curative resolution. Any unauthorized allotment of shares can be ratified by shareholder approval and an amended share register entry.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: CRA registration and tax account setup
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency; Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration for provincial corporate tax registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Apply to the Canada Revenue Agency for a federal Business Number and program accounts, including GST/HST and corporate income tax accounts as required. Register the ULC with the Alberta corporate tax system. For an Alberta ULC, confirm the entity's classification as a corporation and determine whether any unused liability company election is appropriate for cross-border royalty planning.
required_dossiers: Form RC1 Request for a Business Number
Registered office address and mailing address
Pro forma first board resolution appointing tax filing officers
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the CRA requests further information or rejects a program account application, respond to the notice and resubmit the RC1 form with the required supporting documentation. Corporate Tax Act assessments may be administratively reviewed or objected to through the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Confirmation of no physical or municipal operating licence requirement
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Municipal licensing department in the municipality of the registered office, where applicable; Alberta OHS and fire authorities if a physical office is established
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Confirm that the ISIC 6420 IP licensing and patent sub-licensing business is a non-physical, passive holding activity and does not require an Alberta manufacturing or industrial operating permit. If a leased head office is opened, verify municipal business licence requirements, zoning compliance, and building occupancy clearance.
required_dossiers: Registered office confirmation or office lease agreement
Municipal business licence application, if applicable
Zoning or occupancy letter from the landlord or municipality, if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a municipality determines that an office or incidental activity requires a business licence, apply for the licence retroactively to the date of business commencement. Zoning non-conformances may be cured by applying for a minor variance or relocating the registered office.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable - no Alberta industrial or manufacturing licensing authority applies to an intellectual property holding and sub-licensing company
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No statutory operating permit, manufacturing licence, or industrial establishment permit is required under Alberta law for the passive ownership and cross-border sub-licensing of patents and trademarks

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Alberta Environment and Protected Areas - not applicable because the ULC has no physical facility, manufacturing plant, or discharge-producing operation
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt - the ISIC 6420 patent and trademark licensing activity is administrative and passive, not included in the Mandatory or Full EIA categories under the Environmental Assessment Regulation
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not applicable - no wastewater discharge points, VOC emissions sources, or regulated waste streams are created. If incidental office space is leased, waste handling must comply with municipal waste management bylaws and Alberta Recycling Management Regulation standards.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Not applicable for a ULC with no premises. If a leased head office or administrative office is established, fire safety certification under the Alberta Fire Code, structural load and occupancy clearance from the landlord, and a workplace hazard assessment under the Alberta Occupational Health and Safety Code 2009 are required before occupancy.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC) with Business Registration Online (BRO) portal at canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/businesses; provincial counterpart: Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) supported by the Alberta Corporate Registry (Corporate Access Connect).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Incorporate the Alberta Unlimited Liability Corporation under the Alberta Business Corporations Act via Corporate Registry and obtain the Alberta Corporate Access Number. Step 2: Register with CRA for the 9-digit federal Business Number (BN) through the BRO portal or Form RC1, activating program accounts: Corporate Income Tax (RC0001), GST/HST (RT0001), and Payroll (RP0001) if employees exist. Step 3: Since the beneficial owner is non-resident, submit Form RC148 (Application for GST/HST Registration for Non-Resident Registrants) or standard BRO application; a non-resident licensor with no Canadian presence must appoint an authorized representative (RepID) and may be required to provide a Canadian agent for service. Step 4: A non-resident ULC whose only Canadian supply is licensing of patents/trademarks to non-residents is not in the business of carrying on taxable activity in Canada and has no mandatory VAT registration, but may voluntarily register under ETA s. 240 to recover input tax credits (ITCs) for Canadian legal, accounting, and patent-administration costs. Step 5: File the Alberta corporate tax account using the same BN; Alberta imposes no provincial sales tax, so no provincial indirect tax registration exists. Step 6: For treaty-based protection, the ULC files T2 with Schedule 91 and may file NR301 (proof of residency) for the US parent. Step 7: If the ULC is resident in Canada (central management and control in Alberta), it must file T2 corporate returns annually regardless of foreign ownership; any outbound royalty payments to foreign shareholders are subject to Part XIII non-resident withholding tax unless a treaty rate applies.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation_For_Canada: the Alberta ULC is a separate taxpayer under the federal Income Tax Act and the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, resident in Canada where central management and control is exercised, and is NOT a partnership or flow-through for Canadian federal and provincial purposes. Pass_Through_Eligible_For_US_Tax: the ULC's unlimited liability structure qualifies it as an eligible entity under US Treasury Regulation 301.7701-3, allowing a check-the-box election (Form 8832) to treat it as a disregarded entity of a US parent, thereby eliminating Canadian branch tax under the Canada-US Treaty Article XIII(3) and providing US tax symmetry. Territorial_Scope: Canadian-resident ULC taxed on worldwide income, with foreign tax credits and FAPI rules (s. 91-95 ITA); if treated as a US disregarded entity, the CRA may apply treaty article IV(6) fiscally transparent entity rules to attribute income to the US shareholder. Tax_Exempt_Zone: not applicable; Alberta has no special economic zone status, but the ULC is eligible for ordinary deductions, the small business deduction is unavailable (since passive royalty income is not active business income), and no federal patent box regime exists in Canada.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada has no domestic check-the-box election. Available elections and mechanisms: (1) US Form 8832 entity classification election with the IRS, electing disregarded entity or partnership status for the Canadian ULC, commonly combined with a Canada-US Treaty Article IV(6) transparent entity position; (2) CRA elections under the Income Tax Act: s. 216(1) election for non-residents to file a T2 net-basis return on Canadian rental and certain property income, s. 219 branch tax election on repatriated earnings, s. 256(2) affiliated group definitions, and s. 125.7 attestation elections for COVID measures (archived); (3) GST/HST elections: closely related corporation election under ETA s. 156 to zero-rate intercompany supplies, s. 167(2) election for taxable supplies between registrants, s. 227 quick method, and s. 221.1 streamlined accounting; (4) transfer pricing: APA applications, CRA Form T106 reporting election for related-party transactions, and the contemporaneous documentation election under s. 247(4); (5) hybrid mismatch: Canada implemented OECD BEPS Action 2 rules in ss. 18.2-18.4 ITA with no elective regime, but the ULC's unlimited-liability design is itself the standard anti-hybrid solution because US check-the-box on an unlimited liability entity avoids the US foreign hybrid mismatch; a GILTI/Subpart F planning memorandum is recommended to confirm the disposition of the Canadian ULC's income in the US shareholder's hands.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) under Part IX of the Excise Tax Act; Alberta has no provincial sales tax, no HST, and no PST, so only the federal GST applies at the rate of 5% on taxable supplies made in Canada.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 - the small supplier threshold under ETA s. 148(1); a person whose worldwide taxable supplies of goods and services (including zero-rated supplies) are CAD 30,000 or less in the current calendar quarter and in the four preceding calendar quarters is not required to register for GST/HST. A non-resident ULC licensing patents to non-residents has no mandatory registration unless it is deemed to carry on business in Canada or makes taxable supplies in Canada; once the threshold is exceeded or a taxable supply is made in Canada in the course of a Canadian business, mandatory registration under ETA s. 240(1) applies. Voluntary registration under s. 240(2) is permitted for non-residents to claim ITCs, and de-registration is generally prohibited for 12 months after the effective date of registration.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not operate a mandatory real-time fiscal clearance or digital stamping system (no CFDI, e-TIMS, or continuous transaction control regime). Requirements in force: (1) Every GST/HST registrant must issue invoices (ETA ss. 223-224) containing prescribed information: supplier name and BN/RT account, date of invoice, recipient identity, description of supply, amount, GST/HST rate and payable; electronic invoices are permitted with recipient consent but must be retrievable in a legible, auditable format; (2) Mandatory electronic filing: registrants with annual taxable supplies above CAD 1.5 million must file GST/HST returns electronically (GST/HST NETFILE, TELEFILE or EDI); all registrants using reporting accountants must e-file; (3) Peppol-based e-invoicing adoption: the Pan-Canadian E-Invoicing initiative and the Canadian Peppol Authority have published voluntary B2B standards, and federal B2G electronic invoicing through Public Services and Procurement Canada will become mandatory incrementally for selected federal suppliers from 2025-2026, but this is not yet a universal statutory clearance obligation; (4) CRA record retention: registrants must maintain sales and purchase ledgers, source documents, and electronic records in Canada or accessible from Canada in a machine-readable format; CRA may issue compliance orders requiring third-party data via audit API or file access; (5) no XML pre-clearance, no CRA invoice stamping, and no government-run clearance portal is required for royalty invoices; a functionally correct invoice with BN and GST annotation satisfies legal requirements.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: An Alberta-registered ULC IP HoldCo may claim 0% GST on cross-border patent and trademark licensing royalties under Part V of Schedule VI to the Excise Tax Act: (1) Supply of intangible personal property (patent, trademark, copyright, trade secret, or similar incorporeal property) under s. 22, Part V, Schedule VI is zero-rated when supplied to a non-resident person who is not registered under Part IX and is not carrying on business in Canada; the supply is zero-rated regardless of the place of use of the intangible; (2) Supply of a service (licensing administration, patent maintenance, infringement monitoring) under s. 7, Part V, Schedule VI is zero-rated if the recipient is a non-resident and the service is not supplied to a Canadian resident or to a permanent establishment of the non-resident in Canada; (3) A supply to a Canadian resident licensee is taxable at 5% GST in Alberta, and no zero-rating applies to intercompany royalty streams to a Canadian affiliate unless the closely-related election under ETA s. 156 makes the intercorporate supply taxable and zero-rated at the same time for administrative convenience; (4) CRA administrative position: if the ULC has employees or fixed premises in Alberta executing the licenses, it is considered to carry on business in Canada; the non-resident licensor fallback exemption under s. 22 is preserved only if the recipient is a non-resident non-registrant; (5) Documentary proof in an audit is the exporter's burden; a mere contractual recital of non-residency is insufficient without objective evidence; (6) Supplies of goods (if the patent licensing is bundled with tangible deliverables, e.g., prototype units) fall under s. 1, Part V, Schedule VI requiring physical export from Canada within 60 days and retained proof of export; (7) If the zero-rating conditions are not met, the royalty is a taxable supply in Canada subject to 5% GST and, separately, the royalty income may attract Part XIII withholding tax under ss. 212(1)(d) ITA; (8) The ULC can claim full ITCs (input tax credits) for GST paid on Canadian legal, accounting, and patent-renewal fees to the extent the inputs are consumed in making zero-rated supplies, generating a refund position that is normally paid within 4 years under the normal reassessment period.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canada Customs Export Declaration (B13A) filed via the Canadian Export Reporting System / Canadian Automated Export Declaration (CAED) for any physical goods exported in connection with the patent-licensed deliverables, plus the Carrier Certificate or Customs-stamped proof of export and the commercial invoice with Incoterms and value declaration.

Executed patent and trademark license agreement or sub-license agreement, including field-of-use, territory, royalty rate, and payment terms, signed by both parties and indicating that the licensee is a non-resident corporation and is not a GST/HST registrant.
Tax invoice or proforma invoice satisfying ETA s. 223 with the supplier's BN, the annotation '0% GST - Export of Intangible Personal Property under Schedule VI Part V s. 22', and the licence number.

Evidence of non-resident status: certificate of incorporation, foreign tax identification number (TIN), or W-8BEN-E (or equivalent) furnished by the licensee; CRA will not accept self-declarations absent corroboration.

Inward remittance certificate from a Canadian Schedule I bank, SWIFT MT103 credit advice, or intercompany wire confirmation demonstrating actual royalty receipt in the ULC's account; for related-party transactions, transfer pricing documentation under s. 247(4) ITA and a filed Form T106 are mandatory.

CBSA export permits, Controlled Goods Program declarations, or dual-use licence determinations if the licensed patents relate to regulated technologies; applicable export control statements under the Export and Import Permits Act.
Annual GST/HST returns (GST34 or e-file) with the zero-rated supplies schedule and any GST/HST refund claim (Form GST66 or GST189 as applicable) evidencing the net tax position.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA scrutiny is high for zero-rated intercompany royalty structures: (1) limitation period: ETA s. 296 permits reassessment within 4 years for ordinary cases, extended to 6 years where the registrant failed to report zero-rated supplies or made incomplete disclosure, and is unlimited for misrepresentation, fraud, or wilful default; (2) penalties: gross negligence penalty under ETA s. 280 equal to the greater of CAD 500 and 50% of the understated net tax or overclaimed refund; false refund penalty under s. 280.1 of 25% of any refund obtained; failure to file information returns (T106) penalty of CAD 100 per day up to CAD 25,000, with additional penalties for specified foreign reporting under s. 162(10.1); (3) clawback mechanics: upon reassessment CRA denies the zero-rating, treats the royalties as taxable Canadian supplies, requires repayment of the GST refund plus arrears interest at the prescribed rate compounded daily for up to 4 years, and assesses Part XIII withholding tax (25% on royalties to non-residents, reduced to 0% under Article XII(7) of the Canada-US Treaty only if the beneficial owner is a US resident company) plus s. 227(8) penalties of 10% and monthly interest; (4) criminal exposure: s. 239 ETA evasion attracts fines of 50% to 200% of tax evaded and imprisonment up to 5 years; the Customs Act ss. 109-110 imposes penalties for export documentation misstatements; (5) anti-avoidance and hybrid rules: the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (ss. 245 ITA) may recharacterise the entire ULC structure if the principal purpose is to avoid GST or Part XIII; OECD hybrid mismatch rules (ss. 18.2-18.4 ITA) may deny deductions for royalty payments where a US parent's check-the-box election creates a hybrid entity outcome; CRA also audits the substance of the Alberta ULC (board meetings, bank accounts, management decisions, employee activity) to verify whether central management and control is in Canada; (6) practical safe harbour: although Canada has no statutory 180-day FX repatriation requirement, transactional practice and APA norms require documentary proof of actual receipt within 180 days of the deemed accrual to support the economic substance and treaty benefits of the royalty stream; a failure to remit within that window triggers transfer-pricing adjustment risk under s. 247(2), a 10% adjustment penalty under s. 247(3) when the adjustment exceeds CAD 5 million, and potential foreign accrual property income consequences for the US shareholder; (7) mitigating measures: pre-emptive APA or advance GST ruling, contemporaneous TP documentation, CRA voluntary disclosure program (VDP) for self-correction with penalty relief, and legal professional privilege protocols for audit responses.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), acting with the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) for prudential supervision and with FINTRAC for AML/CFT enforcement of the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is freely convertible on both current and capital accounts. Canada maintains a free-floating exchange regime without foreign exchange controls, no central-bank conversion mandate, and no restriction on profit, dividend, or royalty repatriation. The only structural hurdle for an Alberta ULC remitting royalty income to non-residents is Part XIII withholding tax of 25%, generally reduced under the Canada-US treaty (typically 10% for patent royalties), administered through CRA NR301 and NR4/NR6 filings. Capital account transactions such as intercompany loan repayments and equity redemptions are unrestricted but remain subject to the same Part XIII withholding mechanicals where applicable.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada imposes no statutory surrender, conversion timeline, or mandatory ratio on export proceeds, including cross-border royalty and patent licensing receivables. An Alberta ULC may retain foreign-currency receipts in Schedule I bank accounts indefinitely. There is no requirement to repatriate, convert, or escrow export earnings, although IAS 21 translation principles apply for financial reporting.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Low for primary treasury, Medium for ancillary payment rails. Canadian fintech EMIs and money services businesses (Wise, Nuvei, etc.) are registered with FINTRAC and provincially licensed but cannot accept deposits under the Bank Act; they are not substitutes for a Schedule I bank account. An Alberta ULC may use such platforms for low-value disbursements only if a licensed Canadian bank account remains the master concentration account.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Remote onboarding is legally permitted under FINTRAC's updated client identification rules (government-issued ID and digital verification). In practice, Schedule I banks will impose enhanced due diligence on an Alberta ULC with non-resident beneficial owners and cross-border royalty flows; most lenders require a video-escorted interview and notarized or apostilled corporate documents, with a physical branch visit to Calgary or Edmonton requested but not strictly mandated by statute.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident ultimate beneficial ownership of an Alberta ULC with a pure cross-border IP licensing business and limited physical substance.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Alberta Business Corporations Act individual-with-significant-control (ISC) register, certified board resolutions, UBO organizational chart, corporate registry extracts, good standing certificate from Alberta Corporate Registry, CRA business number confirmation, and beneficial-owner passport and proof of address for each director and shareholder.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Royalty payment ratios materially inconsistent with arm's length benchmarks, triggering transfer pricing and tax evasion suspicion.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation per ITA s. 247 and CRA Form T106, fully executed patent and trademark license agreements, CIPO patent registration certificates, independent IP valuation report, economic substance file showing Alberta board meetings and decision-making records, and audited financial statements.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Structuring of payments just below the CAD 10,000 FINTRAC reporting threshold, indicating smurfing or layering.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Written enhanced due diligence policy, no-cash treasury policy, comprehensive SWIFT wire audit trail demonstrating single-transaction royalty payments above threshold, and confirmation from the licensed bank's transaction monitoring that all credits are title-matched to invoiced license fees.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Inbound capital injection with unclear source of funds, particularly where the remitting parent is in a low-tax or high-secrecy jurisdiction.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified banking statements of the remitting shareholder, signed share subscription or intercompany loan agreement, corporate registry evidence of the creditor, sworn source-of-wealth declaration, and if listed, exchange or securities regulator confirmation.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity and shareholder loan proceeds settle via SWIFT MT103 for cross-border wires or via Lynx (formerly LVTS) for CAD domestic concentration. The payment narrative must clearly state the purpose, e.g., 'Shareholder loan drawdown per agreement dated [date] - [entity name] - Alberta ULC - ISIC 6420 IP licensing'; source-of-funds evidence, the underlying financing agreement, and a funds-acknowledgement letter are required by the receiving bank. No Bank of Canada or CRA pre-approval is required for the remittance itself.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Cross-border royalty and license fee payments use SWIFT MT103 with full beneficiary bank SWIFT/BIC and IBAN-equivalent routing. The disbursement must evidence Part XIII withholding through CRA NR4/NR6 filings and form T106 where applicable. For technology and patent acquisition milestones, documentary or standby letters of credit issued under ICC UCP600 and settled through the issuing bank's correspondent network; CAD interbank settlement is cleared via Lynx, with USD cross-border legs routed through CHIPS, Fedwire, or correspondent nostro accounts.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX forwards (CAD/USD, CAD/EUR, CAD/GBP and other freely convertible pairs)
Non-deliverable forwards (CAD vs offshore CNH and restricted-market currencies where the underlying is not deliverable)
Cross-currency swaps (cross-currency interest rate swaps involving CAD and USD or EUR)
FX options and exotic collar structures documenting option premium and strike via an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with Credit Support Annex
Montreal Exchange listed CAD currency futures and futures options

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Alberta Corporate Annual Return (Form Annual Return)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 30 days after the corporation's anniversary date of incorporation annually
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing fee of CAD 50 (approx. USD 37) in addition to the base fee; failure to file for two consecutive fiscal years may result in administrative dissolution of the ULC under the Alberta Business Corporations Act.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (including related provincial allocation and schedules)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 6 months after the end of each fiscal year of the corporation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Penalty of 5% of any unpaid tax for the fiscal year, plus 1% per month for up to 12 months; non-filing may also lead to a demand for return and further court actions without prior notice.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Under the Alberta Business Corporations Act (ABCA), an independent audit is mandatory if: (i) the ULC is a reporting issuer under securities law; (ii) a shareholder or class of shareholders holding at least 5% of the issued voting shares requests an audit in writing; or (iii) federal or Alberta law imposes a specific audit requirement (e.g., financial institution, insurance, or trust activity). For all other private ULCs, the shareholders may pass a unanimous or majority resolution (as provided in the articles) to waive the appointment of an auditor for the fiscal year.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS is mandatory for reporting issuers; a private ULC may elect to apply IFRS or Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE) as permitted by the CPA Canada Handbook. The chosen framework must be consistently applied in preparing annual financial statements.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta ULCs are required to prepare and maintain a register of individuals with significant control (ISC) under the ABCA. The register is not filed annually with the Alberta Corporate Registry, but it must be kept at the registered office and updated within 15 days of any change in significant control, including share transfers affecting ISC. As part of annual maintenance, the corporation should confirm and date-stamp the accuracy of the ISC register in conjunction with the minute book review.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control
Minute Book (including corporate records and by-laws)

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% combined: 15% federal Part I general rate + 8% Alberta provincial general corporate rate; the Alberta ULC is a non-CCPC when controlled by a US parent, so the federal Small Business Deduction rate (9%) is unavailable; no M&P deduction applies to passive patent royalty income.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No patent box, IP regime, or statutory tax holiday exists in Canada. Rate-reducing mechanisms are limited to: (i) s. 126 foreign tax credits for foreign withholding taxes on outbound royalty streams; (ii) SR&ED investment tax credits at 15% non-refundable for qualifying R&D performed in Canada by the ULC; (iii) no Alberta capital tax or payroll tax applies to a passive IP HoldCo.
